## Q1
Match List-I (Network-layer address protocols) with List-II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Address resolution protocol | I. Map physical address to IP address |
| B. Reverse address resolution protocol | II. Used by host and router to send notification of datagram problem back to the sender |
| C. Internet control message protocol | III. Help a multicast router identify hosts in a LAN |
| D. Internet Group message protocol | IV. Map IP address to physical address |

## Q1 - Options
(A) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
(B) A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
(C) A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
(D) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q23

Each protocol resolves one direction of the address mapping or one specific network-layer notification role.

A-IV — Address Resolution Protocol maps a known IP address to the corresponding physical (MAC) address.

B-I — Reverse Address Resolution Protocol does the opposite, mapping a known physical address to an IP address.

C-II — Internet Control Message Protocol carries error and diagnostic notifications, such as an undeliverable datagram, back to the sending host or router.

D-III — Internet Group Management Protocol lets a multicast router discover which hosts on a LAN belong to a multicast group.

A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III is therefore the correct match.

## Q2
Match List-I (IP addresses) with List-II (Address classes).

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. 190.10.75.250 | I. Class E IP address |
| B. 230.41.10.20 | II. Class B IP address |
| C. 242.9.20.80 | III. Class A IP address |
| D. 127.10.125.230 | IV. Class D IP address |

## Q2 - Options
(A) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
(B) A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
(C) A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III
(D) A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q61

IP address classes are determined by the value of the first octet.

A. 190.10.75.250 falls in the 128–191 range, which is Class B, so A pairs with II.<br>
B. 230.41.10.20 falls in the 224–239 range, which is Class D (multicast), so B pairs with IV.<br>
C. 242.9.20.80 falls in the 240–255 range, which is Class E, so C pairs with I.<br>
D. 127.10.125.230 falls in the 0–127 range, which is conventionally taught as Class A, so D pairs with III.

This gives A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

## Q5
A class B network on the Internet has a subnet mask of 255.255.248.0, what is the maximum number of hosts per subnet?

## Q5 - Options
(A) 1022
(B) 1023
(C) 2046
(D) 2047

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q58

The mask 255.255.248.0 is 11111111.11111111.11111000.00000000, leaving 11 zero bits for the host field. That gives 2¹¹ = 2048 addresses per subnet, less the network and broadcast addresses, so 2046 usable hosts — option C.

## Q6
Two computers A and B are configured as follows<br>
: A has IP address 203.197.2.53 and subnet mask<br>

**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q69

**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q80

## Q9
Which protocol is used to acquire the MAC Address of a host whose IP address is known?

## Q9 - Options
(A) Dynamic Host control protocol
(B) Address Resolution Protocol
(C) Reverse Address Resolution Protocol
(D) User Datagram Protocol

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q33

The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) broadcasts a request containing a known IP address and receives back the corresponding MAC address of the host that owns it, which is exactly the direction of lookup described here.

Reverse ARP does the opposite lookup, finding an IP address from a known MAC address, DHCP assigns IP configuration to hosts, and UDP is a transport-layer protocol unrelated to address resolution, so ARP is the only option that matches IP-to-MAC resolution.

## Q10
Consider the routing table of an organization's router.

Which of the following prefixes in CIDR notation can be collectively used to correctly aggregate all of the subnets in the routing table?

A. 12.20.164.0/20<br>
B. 12.20.164.0/22<br>
C. 12.20.164.0/21<br>
D. 12.20.168.0/22

Choose the correct answer:

| Subnet Number | Subnet Mask | Next Hop |
|---|---|---|
| 12.20.164.0 | 255.255.252.0 | R1 |
| 12.20.170.0 | 255.255.254.0 | R2 |
| 12.20.168.0 | 255.255.254.0 | Interface 0 |
| 12.20.166.0 | 255.255.254.0 | Interface 1 |
| Default | — | R3 |

Organization router's subnet table

## Q10 - Options
(A) A and B Only
(B) A and C Only
(C) C and D Only
(D) B and D Only

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q61

Converting each mask to its block of covered third-octet values shows the routing table actually covers the continuous range 164 through 171, once the overlap between rows is accounted for.

12.20.164.0/255.255.252.0 is a /22, an aligned 4-value block covering 164-167. 12.20.170.0/255.255.254.0 is a /23, a 2-value block covering 170-171. 12.20.168.0/255.255.254.0 is a /23 covering 168-169. 12.20.166.0/255.255.254.0 is a /23 covering 166-167, which is already fully contained inside the first row's 164-167 block.

The true union of all four rows is therefore the range 164-171, eight consecutive third-octet values. This range is not itself a single power-of-two-aligned block starting at 164, since a true /21 (8-value) block starting at 164 would need 164 to be a multiple of 8, which it is not.

Instead, this exact 8-value range splits cleanly into two valid /22 blocks: 12.20.164.0/22 (164-167, aligned since 164 is a multiple of 4) and 12.20.168.0/22 (168-171, aligned since 168 is a multiple of 4). Together these two prefixes exactly cover 164-171 with no wasted address space, matching options B and D, while option A's /20 wrongly stretches the range down to 160 and up to 175, and option C's /21 is not properly aligned to start at 164.

## Q12
An organization is granted the block 130.56.0.0/16. The administrator wants to create 1024 subnets.

What will be the prefix length of each subnet?

## Q12 - Options
(A) /24
(B) /25
(C) /26
(D) /27

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q92

Creating 1024 equal subnets from a /16 block requires borrowing enough host bits to distinguish 1024 subnets.

1024 = 2^10, so 10 bits must be borrowed from the host portion.

New prefix length = 16 + 10 = /26

The official answer key for this exact sitting lists a different option here, but that would require a /24 prefix (256 addresses per subnet), which directly contradicts the same key's own confirmed answer to the "addresses per subnet" question in this set (64 addresses, which only a /26 prefix produces). Because those two answers cannot both be correct for the same subnetting scenario, /26 is kept here as the internally consistent answer, and this conflict is noted for a human to double-check against the original key.

## Q15
An organization is granted the block 130.56.0.0/16. The administrator wants to create 1024 subnets.

Find the subnet mask.

## Q15 - Options
(A) 255.255.255.0
(B) 255.255.255.128
(C) 255.255.255.192
(D) 255.255.255.224

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q95

A /26 prefix sets the first 26 bits of the address to 1, which spans all of the first three octets plus the top two bits of the fourth octet.

The fourth octet's top two bits set gives 11000000 in binary, which is 192 in decimal.

The subnet mask is 255.255.255.192.

NTA's official final answer key for this exact sitting marked this question as dropped (full marks awarded to all candidates). The mask 255.255.255.192 is the direct, unambiguous consequence of the confirmed /26 prefix used elsewhere in this same question set, so the drop does not appear to reflect any ambiguity in the mask itself.

## Q18
Which of the following class of IP address has the last address as 223.255.255.255?

## Q18 - Options
(A) Class A
(B) Class B
(C) Class C
(D) Class D

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q89

Classful IPv4 addressing defines the primary address ranges based on high-order bits:

- Class A spans from 0.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255 (leading bit 0).
- Class B spans from 128.0.0.0 to 191.255.255.255 (leading bits 10).
- Class C spans from 192.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255 (leading bits 110).
- Class D spans from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 (leading bits 1110).

Consequently, Class C concludes at 223.255.255.255.

## Q20
You need 500 subnets, each with about 100 usable host addresses per subnet. What network mask will you assign using a class B network address?

## Q20 - Options
(A) 255-255-255-252
(B) 255-255-255-128
(C) 255-255-255-0
(D) 255-255-254-0

## Q20 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q28

A Class B network provides 16 host bits with a default /16 mask.

Determining required bit allocations:

1. 500 subnets require s subnet bits where 2^s &gt;= 500, giving s = 9 bits (2^9 = 512 subnets).
2. 100 usable hosts require h host bits where 2^h - 2 &gt;= 100, giving h = 7 bits (2^7 - 2 = 126 hosts).<br>
    Total bits s + h = 9 + 7 = 16 bits.

Adding 9 subnet bits to the 16 network bits produces a /25 mask:<br>
First three octets = 255.255.255<br>
Fourth octet = 10000000 in binary = 128.<br>
Resulting mask is 255-255-255-128.

## Q21
What percentage (%) of the IPv4, IP address space do all class C addresses consume?

## Q21 - Options
(A) 12.5%
(B) 25%
(C) 37.5%
(D) 50%

## Q21 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q72

In classful IPv4 addressing, leading bit prefixes allocate total address space proportions:

- Class A starts with 0 (1/2 of space = 50%).
- Class B starts with 10 (1/4 of space = 25%).
- Class C starts with 110 (1/8 of space = 12.5%).
- Class D starts with 1110 (1/16 of space = 6.25%).
- Class E starts with 1111 (1/16 of space = 6.25%).

Class C networks account for 12.5% of all IPv4 addresses.

## Q22
Consider the following two statements with respect to IPv4 in computer networking:<br>
P: The loopback (IP) address is a member of class B network.<br>
Q: The loopback (IP) address is used to send a packet from host to itself.

What can you say about the statements P and Q?

## Q22 - Options
(A) P-True; Q-False
(B) P-False; Q-True
(C) P-True; Q-True
(D) P-False; Q-False

## Q22 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q91

Evaluating IPv4 loopback network properties:

- **P** is false because the entire 127.0.0.0/8 address block is designated for loopback testing. In classful addressing, first-octet values from 0 through 127 fall under Class A, not Class B (Class B ranges from 128 to 191).
- **Q** is true because loopback packets short-circuit within the host network stack, allowing a machine to transmit IP packets directly to its own services without placing frames onto physical network media.

Thus, P is false and Q is true.

## Q23
An Internet Service Provider (ISP) has following chunk of CIDR-based IP addresses available with it : 245.248.128.0/20. The ISP wants to give half of this chunk of addresses to organization A and a quarter to organization B while retaining the remaining with itself. Which of the following is a valid allocation of addresses to A and B ?

## Q23 - Options
(A) 245.248.136.0/21 and 245.248.128.0/22
(B) 245.248.128.0/21 and 245.248.128.0/22
(C) 245.248.132.0/22 and 245.248.132.0/21
(D) 245.248.136.0/24 and 245.248.132.0/21

## Q23 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q61

Subdividing a /20 block assigns a /21 prefix for half the address space and a /22 prefix for a quarter without address collision.

- The initial block is 245.248.128.0/20 (spanning third-octet values 128 through 143).
- Giving half to organization A requires a /21 mask (covering 8 third-octet values):<br>
    Half 1: 245.248.128.0/21 (octets 128 to 135)<br>
    Half 2: 245.248.136.0/21 (octets 136 to 143)
- Giving a quarter to organization B requires a /22 mask (covering 4 third-octet values) from the unused half:<br>
    From Half 1: 245.248.128.0/22 (octets 128 to 131) and 245.248.132.0/22 (octets 132 to 135).
- In Option A, organization A receives 245.248.136.0/21 and organization B receives 245.248.128.0/22.
- These two allocations are mutually disjoint subsets of the parent block, leaving 245.248.132.0/22 (the remaining quarter) for the ISP.
- Option B produces overlapping allocations where B is inside A.
- Option C and Option D feature invalid prefix lengths or overlapping segments.

## Q24
The four byte IP Address consists of

## Q24 - Options
(A) Network Address
(B) Both Network and Host Addresses
(C) Host Address
(D) Neither Network nor Host Address

## Q24 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Subnetting & IP Addressing
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q72

In IPv4 architecture, a 4-byte (32-bit) address is partitioned into a network prefix and a host identifier.

- The Network Address (Network ID) identifies the specific network or subnetwork on which the host resides.
- The Host Address (Host ID) identifies the individual network interface card on that specific network.
- Both parts are essential for routing packets between disparate networks and delivering them to the destination device.
- Therefore, it consists of both Network and Host Addresses (Option B).
